Visualizer for Plex

Does Plex have a visualizer on Mac?

By Syd Lawrence, a visual artist and developer who makes Vibresia. Facts last checked 2 November 2026; updated 2 November 2026.

Partly. Plex does have visualisers, and they are good ones: they live in Plexamp, the music player, and in the mobile apps, and Plex lists them as a Plex Pass premium music feature. What they do not do is appear in the Plex desktop app for Mac or in the Plex web player, which is where a lot of people play their library on a Mac. If you play Plex in Plexamp, use Plex's own. If you play it in the desktop app or in a browser, an app that listens to the Mac's system audio works with all of them: Vibresia, which we make, does that for free.

Plex on a Mac
Built-in visualiserYes. Plex lists visualisers as a Plex Pass premium music feature, in the apps that support them.
On a MacPlex has a native Mac desktop app, with more robust playback than its web app.
In a browserPlex plays in a browser through the Plex Web App player, which comes with Plex Media Server and needs no extra software.

Where Plex's visualisers are, and where they aren't

Plex's own documentation puts visualisers in the apps that support them: Plexamp, its music player, which advertises over a dozen of them, and the mobile app, where the visualiser is dynamic and follows the track being played. Both need Plex Pass. Plex says the visualisers are driven straight from the audio engine, so they react to the music rather than to a beat clock.

The gap is on a Mac. Plex's list of the Plex Web App player controls covers playback, quality, audio, subtitles, chapters and the play queue, with no visualiser among them, and the documentation for the Plex desktop app for Mac lists player settings for audio and subtitles and download settings, with no visualiser there either. Searching Plex's own support library for visualisers turns up the iOS player, Plex Music, licence information and the Plex Pass feature list, and nothing about the web or Mac players.

An app that listens to the Mac's system audio does not have that gap. It does not need to know Plex exists: whatever Plex is playing, the app hears it, and the visuals follow, whether it came from Plexamp, the desktop app or a tab in the browser.

How to get visuals for Plex on a Mac

Vibresia is a free Mac app that listens to the Mac's system audio, so it doesn't need Plex to support it. Install it, allow it to hear system audio the first time it asks, and play something in Plex. The visuals follow the music straight away: it picks out the beat, the bass, mids and treble and the tempo on the Mac, and nothing is uploaded.

It has 18 built-in scenes, and Auto Scan moves between them on the beat. If you want something of your own, a scene is a single GLSL function, or you can describe one to an AI assistant and have it written for you. It needs macOS 14.2 or later, Apple silicon.

Why system audio is the way to do it

A visualiser built into one music app only sees that app. Apple's own visualiser is a good example: it only works with songs playing in the Music app. Listening to the Mac's system audio instead means one visualiser works with Plex, with every other music app, with a browser tab and with a film, and keeps going when you switch between them.

Questions people ask

Does Plex have a visualizer?

Yes, in Plexamp and the mobile apps, where they are a Plex Pass premium music feature. The Plex desktop app for Mac and the Plex web player do not list one.

Is there a Plex app for Mac?

Yes, a native desktop app alongside the Plex web player, which runs in the browser. Plex Media Player is also available for Mac as a home theatre player.

Do I need Plex Pass for the visualisers?

For Plex's own, yes: Plex lists them as a Plex Pass premium music feature.

Is Vibresia free?

Yes. Every feature is free, with no account and no trial, and the code is open source under the MIT licence.
